intro.html: Time can be wasted, saved, stretched or rushed, and English has a word for each. This topic moves from the slow end (putting things off, dawdling, lingering) through pauses and rests to the fast end (hurrying, and hurrying too much).

Putting off: procrastinate, defer. Too slow: dawdle, linger, dilatory, belated. Pauses: a hiatus (a break in an activity), a respite (a rest from something hard). Fast: hasten (hurry) and precipitate (too hasty, without thinking).

Watch two words with double lives. defer means to put off, but also to give way to someone wiser (“I defer to the expert”). precipitate as an adjective means rash and hasty; as a verb it means to bring about suddenly.

words.def: to keep putting off something one should do
words.ex: If you {procrastinate} on your science project, you’ll be gluing it together at midnight.
words.ctx: Maya knew the essay was due Monday, yet she continued to {procrastinate}, cleaning her room, sorting her books and baking cookies instead of writing a single word.
words.etym: From Latin procrastinare, “to put off till tomorrow”: pro- (forward) + crastinus (of tomorrow), from cras (tomorrow).

mn.text: The homework pile grows taller, but Pip keeps playing and saying, “Tomorrow!” He pushes everything to tomorrow: he {procrastinates}.

scene.alt: A boy plays on a laptop, saying “Tomorrow!”, next to a big pile of homework and a calendar marked DUE.

words.def: to put off until later; also, to give way to another’s judgment
words.ex: The club agreed to {defer} the vote until everyone could attend.
words.ctx: Though he had strong opinions about the garden, Kai chose to {defer} to his grandmother, who had grown tomatoes for fifty years and knew far more than he did.
words.etym: Two Latin verbs met in this word: differre, “to put off,” and deferre, “to carry down, to yield.”
words.note: To defer to someone is to give way to their judgment, out of respect: “I’ll defer to the coach.”

mn.cue: de-FER: carry it FAR off, to later
mn.text: Too busy today, Ada pushes the big cleanup box far off down the hall and writes “next week” on the calendar: she {defers} it.

scene.alt: A woman pushes a big box of work away toward next week on the calendar.

words.def: to waste time; to move slowly and idly
words.ex: Don’t {dawdle}; the bus leaves in five minutes!
words.ctx: Instead of hurrying home as they had promised, the boys {dawdled}, skipping stones at the creek and watching ducks until the sun went down.

mn.text: On the way to school, Kai stops to poke every puddle, smell every flower and count every snail while Mom waits up ahead: he {dawdles}.

scene.alt: A boy kneels to look at a snail on the way to school while his mother waits impatiently.

words.def: to stay longer than needed; to be slow to leave
words.ex: The smell of fresh bread {lingered} in the kitchen all afternoon.
words.ctx: Long after the concert ended, a few fans {lingered} by the stage door, unwilling to leave until they had seen the band one last time.

mn.text: The party ended at nine, but Uncle Omar stays at the door telling one more story, then another, longer and longer: he {lingers}.

scene.alt: At night, a guest keeps chatting at the doorway while his sleepy host yawns.

words.ex: The {dilatory} repair crew took three months to fix one pothole.
words.ctx: The committee’s {dilatory} approach frustrated everyone; it held meeting after meeting, putting off the decision again and again, while the old bridge kept crumbling.

mn.text: The waiter strolls, stops to read the paper, then dilly-dallies some more while the hungry diners watch the clock: he is {dilatory}.

scene.alt: A waiter reads the newspaper while a hungry customer waits and waits.

words.ex: Grandpa sent me a {belated} birthday card with an apology for being late.
words.ctx: The thank-you note was {belated}, arriving a full two months after the party, but Aunt Lin was happy to get it all the same.

mn.cue: BE-LATE-d: LATE, but here at last
mn.text: A week after Zoe’s birthday, Pip runs up with a card: “Happy birthday… last week!” His wishes are {belated}.

scene.alt: A boy sheepishly hands a girl a birthday card a week late.

words.def: a break or pause in an activity
words.ex: The band went on {hiatus} for a year while its members traveled.
words.ctx: After a two-year {hiatus}, during which the old theater was closed for repairs, the town’s summer plays finally returned.
words.etym: From Latin hiatus, “an opening, a gap,” from hiare (to gape).

mn.cue: HI-ATUS: a GAP in the show
mn.text: The stage sits empty under a sign that says BACK IN JUNE, and only the theater cat is performing, by napping: the show is on {hiatus}.

scene.alt: An empty stage with a sign reading BACK IN JUNE and a cat napping in the spotlight.

words.def: a short rest or relief from something hard
words.ex: The shady oak offered a brief {respite} from the heat.
words.ctx: The storm raged for three days, but on Tuesday afternoon there was a short {respite}: the rain stopped for an hour, and everyone rushed out to buy groceries.
words.etym: From Old French respit, “delay,” from Latin respectus (a looking back).

mn.text: After three hot hours on the trail, the hikers flop down in the cool shade of a tree for a short rest: a welcome {respite}.

scene.alt: Two tired hikers rest happily in the cool shade of a tree on a hot day.

words.def: to hurry; to make something happen sooner
words.ex: We {hastened} home when we saw the dark clouds.
words.ctx: Warm, sunny weather will {hasten} the tomatoes’ ripening, while a cold spell will slow it down.

mn.text: The bus is pulling up, and Dev makes haste down the street with his backpack bouncing: he {hastens} to catch it.

scene.alt: A teen with a backpack runs fast to catch a bus.

words.def: done suddenly and without careful thought; hasty
words.ex: Selling the house after one bad day was a {precipitate} decision.
words.ctx: The coach warned against any {precipitate} changes after a single loss; she wanted to study the game film carefully before deciding anything.
words.etym: From Latin praecipitare, “to throw headlong,” from praeceps (headlong): prae- (forward) + caput (head).
words.note: As a verb (prih-SIP-ih-tayt), precipitate means to bring about suddenly: the snub precipitated a quarrel.

mn.text: One raindrop lands on Grandpa’s nose, and he cancels the whole picnic at once without even looking at the sunny sky: his decision is {precipitate}.

scene.alt: On a sunny day, a grandfather feels one drop and shouts to cancel the picnic while a girl shrugs.

head: slow
pause
fast
rows: procrastinate: put it off and off
hiatus: a break in an activity
respite: a rest from something hard
dilatory: slow to act; belated: late
after.cap: From the slow end to the fast end.

after.html: defer has two meanings. To defer a decision is to postpone it; to defer to a person is to give way to their judgment, as Kai does when he defers to his grandmother about tomatoes. The noun for the second sense is deference.

after.name: vo-cloze

opts.s: After weeks of nonstop rain, the sunny weekend was a welcome {respite}.

after.cap: A short relief from something unpleasant is a respite.

items.q: In which sentence does defer mean “give way to someone else’s judgment”?
choices: On questions about the boat, the crew always defers to the captain.
The school will defer the field trip until spring.
They deferred the meeting because of the snow.
items.why: To defer to someone is to yield to their judgment. The other two sentences use the “put off” sense.

items.q: Quitting the team after one bad practice would be a ______ decision. Which word fits?
items.why: A sudden decision made without careful thought is precipitate.

items.q: True or false: to procrastinate is to keep putting off a task.
items.why: True. The Latin cras means tomorrow: a procrastinator always says “tomorrow.”

items.q: The TV show made no new episodes for two years, then came back with a new season. During those two years, the show was on…
items.why: A break in an activity is a hiatus. A respite is relief from something hard or unpleasant.
